title: Star Trails over SOAR
caption: Star trails above the SOAR Telescope, Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory
celestial: Landscape photograph; the source does not name the site

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Shortly before sunrise, stars appear to trail in circles above the Southern Astrophysical Research (SOAR) Telescope. At the center of the circles lies the south celestial pole. A few airplanes, shooting stars and satellites have left faint trails as well. SOAR belongs to NSF NOIRLab's Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory.

The trails come from the rotation of Earth. Over a long exposure, the turning planet makes each star smear into an arc across the frame, and the arcs grow longer the longer the camera keeps collecting light.

Research telescopes cannot accept that smearing. To produce sharp images of stars, planets and galaxies, instruments like SOAR rely on sophisticated tracking and guiding systems that follow their targets precisely, sometimes for hours at a time. Combined with adaptive optics, which correct for the blurring caused by the atmosphere, these systems let modern telescopes make clear images of every type of celestial object.

understand.summary: A long-exposure night photograph by M. Paredes. No camera or exposure details or color mapping are published.
understand.eye: The eye sees stars as fixed points, and the trails appear only because the camera kept recording while Earth turned.
